question: A 44-year-old man with HIV comes to the physician for a routine follow-up examination. He has been noncompliant with his antiretroviral medication regimen for several years. He appears chronically ill and fatigued. CD4+ T-lymphocyte count is 405/mm3 (N ≥ 500). Further evaluation of this patient is most likely to show which of the following findings?

paths: (Chronic Disease)-CAUSES->(arterial stiffness)-PROCESS_OF->(Bone structure of lumbar vertebra)-LOCATION_OF->(Chest CT)

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Noncompliance with antiretroviral medication -> decreased CD4+ T-lymphocyte count -> 80% CHAIN: Decreased CD4+ T-lymphocyte count -> increased risk of opportunistic infections -> 90% CHAIN: Increased risk of opportunistic infections -> possible multifocal demyelination on brain MRI -> 70% CHAIN: Possible multifocal demyelination on brain MRI -> ring-enhancing lesions on brain MRI -> 60% CHAIN: Ring-enhancing lesions on brain MRI -> 40% CHAIN: Noncompliance with antiretroviral medication -> chronic illness and fatigue -> 70% CHAIN: Chronic illness and fatigue -> possible ground-glass opacities on chest CT -> 80%
enhanced_information: Noncompliance with antiretroviral medication in a patient with HIV can lead to decreased CD4+ T-lymphocyte count, increasing the risk of opportunistic infections. This patient's presentation of chronic illness and fatigue suggests a possible ground-glass opacities finding on chest CT due to potential pulmonary involvement. The most likely finding in further evaluation would be ground-glass opacities on chest CT.
analysis: Noncompliance with antiretroviral medication in a patient with HIV can lead to decreased CD4+ T-lymphocyte count, increasing the risk of opportunistic infections. The patient's presentation of chronic illness and fatigue suggests potential pulmonary involvement. Ground-glass opacities on chest CT are commonly seen in HIV-related pulmonary infections. While other findings like violaceous skin lesions (Kaposi sarcoma), cotton-wool spots (CMV retinitis), multifocal demyelination, and ring-enhancing lesions (toxoplasmosis) can occur in HIV patients, the most likely finding in this case would be ground-glass opacities on chest CT.
